extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners studying MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, framing, and making nonstatutory (including obviousness-type and Schneller-type) double patenting rejections during patent examination, including when to use provisional vs. actual rejections, required analyses, form paragraphs, and related statutory rejections under pre-AIA and AIA law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and definition of nonstatutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on nonstatutory double patenting is a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy so as to prevent the unjustified or improper timewise extension of the right to exclude granted by a patent and to prevent possible harassment by multiple assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonstatutory double patenting is appropriate where the claims at issue are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). See cited cases (In re Berg; In re Goodman; In re Longi; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting (ODP) trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis parallels 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness determinations (Graham factors). The patent underlying the double patenting rejection is not considered prior art for 103, but the same factual inquiries apply. Form paragraphs (e.g., 8.36, 8.34, 8.35) are available for use depending on whether the reference is a patent or a copending application and whether secondary references are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries for obviousness-type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries when determining obviousness-type double patenting: (A) determine the scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) determine the differences between the scope and content of the patent claim and the application claim; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (D) evaluate any objective indicia of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conclusion of obviousness-type double patenting is made in light of these factual determinations. Examiner should articulate these issues when making an ODP rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required explanation in an obviousness-type double patenting rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (A) the differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims — a claim in the patent compared to a claim in the application; and (B) the reasons why a person of ordinary skill in the art would conclude that the invention defined in the claim at issue is anticipated by, or would have been an obvious variation of, the invention defined in a claim in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit rationale tying claim differences to why the application claim is anticipated or an obvious variation. If relying on an obviousness rationale, insert an explanation of the obviousness analysis (bracketed text guidance appears in form paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the patent disclosure in ODP analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of the patent may not be used as prior art for obviousness; however, the specification can be used as a dictionary to learn the meaning of a claim term and those portions of the specification which provide support for the patent claims may be examined and considered when addressing whether a claim in the application defines an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the portion of the patent disclosure that pertains to the invention claimed in the patent supports the patent claims and may be considered. Courts recognize it is difficult to define 'obvious variation' categorically; focus on whether the application claim is an obvious variation of an embodiment disclosed in the patent that supports the patent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way vs two-way obviousness test
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application at issue is the later filed application or both are filed on the same day, only a one-way determination of obviousness is needed. A two-way test is applied only when the patent is the later filed application and the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and there is administrative delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-way test: consider whether the application claim would have been anticipated by or an obvious variation of the patent claim. Two-way test: apply the Graham analysis twice (application vs patent and patent vs application); an ODP rejection is appropriate only where each analysis compels a conclusion of obviousness. Absent clear administrative delay and inability to have filed claims together, examiners may use the one-way test and shift burden to applicant to show two-way required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative delay and burden to justify two-way test
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-way determination is only appropriate where (A) there was administrative delay on the part of the Office causing delay in prosecution of the earlier-filed application; and (B) applicant could not have filed the conflicting claims in a single (earlier-filed) application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record does not clearly show administrative delay and inability to have filed claims together, apply one-way test. Courts examine the reasons for delay (applicant-requested extensions, abandonments, appeals, interferences) to decide responsibility for delay. Examples: Berg, Emert, Pierce, General Foods.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to make additional statutory rejections (pre-AIA and AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, make a rejection under the relevant statutory provisions (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g)/102(e)/103(a) or AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 103) in addition to or instead of a nonstatutory double patenting rejection depending on inventive entities, filing dates, and whether the reference is prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If the patent is to a different inventive entity and has an earlier effective U.S. filing date, a pre-AIA 102(e)/103(a) rejection may be appropriate using form paragraph 7.21.02.fti. For AIA examinations, consider 102(a)(2)/103 rejections if appropriate. Do not make statutory rejections that are precluded (e.g., if patent disqualified under 103(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejections (copending applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection when the patentably indistinct claims are in a copending application rather than an issued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 8.33 must precede provisional paragraphs (8.35 or 8.37). The provisional rejection should also be made in the reference application. Use 8.35 (no secondary references) or 8.37 (with secondary references) as applicable. Insert explanations of the obviousness analysis in bracketed areas. Additional statutory rejections may also be required depending on inventive entities and filing dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph and heading usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.33 (heading) must precede any one of form paragraphs 8.34 to 8.39 and must be used only ONCE in an Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate follow-on form paragraph depending on whether the reference is a patent or copending application, whether secondary references are cited, and whether pre-AIA or AIA law applies. Follow bracket insertion guidance (which brackets to fill with patent number, application number, obviousness explanation, secondary references, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for using terminal disclaimers to overcome ODP
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or 1.321(d) (and signed per 1.321(b)) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory double patenting ground provided the reference application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with this application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO provides terminal disclaimer forms (including eTerminal Disclaimer). The filing date determines which form to use. See MPEP §1490 for guidance regarding terminal disclaimers and withdrawal of ODP rejections when terminal disclaimer is the only remaining rejection. Note limitations (priority/benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119 not considered for earlier-filed determination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership / inventive entity / joint research agreement considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstatutory double patenting form paragraphs may be used where the patentably indistinct invention is claimed in a patent or copending application that is: (a) by the same inventive entity; or (b) by a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned even though there is no common inventor; or (c) not commonly assigned but has at least one inventor in common; or (d) made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement (pre-AIA 103 context) ; or (e) under AIA, commonly owned or deemed commonly owned under specified AIA provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the proper factual predicate for common ownership or joint research agreement. If file does not establish common ownership at the relevant time, use additional form paragraphs (e.g., 8.28.fti) to resolve priority or benefit issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to make provisional rejections in the reference application
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection should also be made in the reference (copending) application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using provisional rejection form paragraphs (8.35/8.37), the examiner should also make a corresponding provisional rejection in the copending reference application to ensure consistent treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schneller-type (other) nonstatutory double patenting — rare circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: There are unique circumstances (illustrated by In re Schneller) where a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is applicable even where the two or more inventions are considered nonobvious over each other — i.e., where allowance of the later claims would unjustifiably extend patent protection based on the particular facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schneller-type rejections are rare and limited to particular factual situations; the Technology Center Director must approve any Schneller-based nonstatutory double patenting rejection. Examiner should first consult with the SPE, and if SPE agrees, obtain TC Director approval before making such a rejection. Each situation must be decided on its own facts; courts cautioned against generalizing Schneller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way ODP application procedure and consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a two-way obviousness determination is required, apply the Graham analysis twice, once with the application claims as the claims in issue, and once with the patent claims as the claims in issue; an obvious-type double patenting rejection is appropriate only where each analysis compels a conclusion that the invention defined in the claims in issue is an obvious variation of the invention defined in a claim in the other application/patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either analysis does not compel obviousness, no obviousness-type double patenting rejection is made (though other nonstatutory double patenting bases may apply). Use form paragraphs 8.33 and appropriate follow-on paragraphs; document analyses carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketing and content insertion guidance for form paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs contain bracketed placeholders that must be filled with specifics: e.g., bracket 3 for patent or application number, bracket 4 for the obviousness rationale or secondary reference, bracket 5 for explanation of the obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Examiner Notes accompanying each form paragraph for detailed instructions (which paragraphs apply depending on patent vs application, AIA vs pre-AIA, presence of secondary references, and when additional statutory rejections should be made).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority/benefit claims and determination of earlier-filed application for double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority or benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a) and (e) are not taken into account in determining which is the earlier-filed application for double patenting purposes (both for pre-AIA and AIA contexts, as noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult MPEP §1490 and the specific AIA/pre-AIA paragraphs for guidance when terminal disclaimers or withdrawal of ODP rejections are at issue; be mindful that benefit claims do not alter the earlier-filed determination used for ODP analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to add provisional pre-AIA 102(e) rejection for different inventive entity and effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applications do not have the same inventive entity and effective U.S. filing date, a provisional pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection should additionally be made in the later-filed application using form paragraph 7.15.01.fti.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the additional statutory rejection where the factual predicate (different inventive entity and effective filing date) is met. Follow guidance on when to include pre-AIA statutory rejections and when they are foreclosed by 103(c) disqualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: For AIA examinations: use of form paragraph 8.27.aia and concurrent statutory rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications being examined under the AIA: If the patent is to a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned with the application, form paragraph 8.27.aia should additionally be used to request that the applicant take action to amend or cancel claims such that the applications no longer contain claims directed to the same invention. A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 35 U.S.C. 103 should also be made if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is no evidence of common ownership as of the effective filing date, additional form paragraphs (e.g., 8.28.aia) may be used. Ensure concurrent statutory rejections are made where the reference qualifies as prior art under AIA provisions.
